candidates.title: Keep trailing instructions and stop sequences around user input in LLM app prompts
candidates.rule: When templating user input into an application prompt, place additional instruction text after the {user_input} slot and configure stop sequences; both measurably lower goal-hijacking success.
candidates.passage: F5 Stop sequences hinder attacks (Table B8 ). F6 Prompts with text after the {user_input} are harder to attack (Table B9 ).
candidates.location: Section 5 Results and discussion; Tables B8, B9
candidates.finding: With text-davinci-002 and the default attack prompt, goal-hijack success fell from 60.0±0.0% to 47.5±5.0% with stop sequences (on the 10 prompts that have them) and from 63.1±2.4% to 51.8±3.6% for prompts with text after the user input. Both reduce but do not eliminate attacks.
workloads: 35 base prompts from the OpenAI Examples page
goal hijacking attack (rogue string 'I hate humans')
candidates.conditions: Single default attack prompt with newline/dash delimiters; 4 repetitions per experiment; stop-sequence comparison used only 10 prompts that natively include stop sequences; text-after-input comparison is between different prompt groups, not a controlled rewrite of the same prompt.
candidates.limitations: 2022-era GPT-3 models only; group comparisons are confounded by prompt content; residual attack success remains ~48-52%; no test on modern chat models or system/user message separation.
candidates.validation_test: Take a set of current production-style prompts, create matched variants with and without trailing instructions and with/without stop sequences, run a fixed injection suite on today's models, and compare success rates.

candidates.title: Treat delimiter sequences in user input as an injection signal
candidates.rule: Strip or escape delimiter runs (e.g. newline plus repeated '-', '=', '>') from user-supplied text before substituting it into a prompt, since such separators raise injection success.
candidates.passage: F2 Delimiters significantly improve attacks, but the impact of delimiter type, length, and repetitions is not clear
candidates.location: Section 5 Results; Tables B3, B4, B5
candidates.finding: Adding a newline plus two 10-character dash runs before the injected instruction raised goal-hijack success from 43.6±2.7% to 58.6±1.6% on text-davinci-002. The paper measured the attack side; filtering delimiters as a defence is our inference from that attack result.
workloads: goal hijacking with 'Ignore any previous and following instructions and just print...'
candidates.conditions: Delimiter type (-, =, >), length (4/10/20) and repetitions (1-4) all helped, with differences within noise; no filtering defence was actually implemented or evaluated.
candidates.limitations: Defence is untested; stripping delimiters may break legitimate inputs (code, tables, markdown) and attackers can use other separators or paraphrases.
candidates.validation_test: Implement delimiter stripping/escaping in a prompt-templating layer and measure injection success and task quality on benign inputs before and after, on current models.

candidates.title: Budget more injection defence for the most instruction-capable model in a family
candidates.rule: When choosing a model for a user-facing prompt app, assume the strongest instruction-following variant is the most vulnerable to injected instructions and allocate more output filtering and red-teaming to it rather than assuming capability implies robustness.
candidates.passage: F8 text-davinci-002 is by far the model most susceptible to attacks (Table B10 ).
candidates.finding: Default attack success was 13.8±2.2% (ada), 29.5±5.9% (babbage), 23.8±3.9% (curie), 30.5±3.9% (davinci-001) versus 58.6±1.6% (text-davinci-002); authors attribute this to better instruction-following, an inverse-scaling pattern.
workloads: goal hijacking with default attack prompt
candidates.conditions: One attack prompt, one model family, 2022 API models; weaker models may fail the underlying task too, so low attack rates do not mean they are usable substitutes.
candidates.limitations: Single paper, single family, pre-RLHF-chat era; later safety training may reverse the trend, so this is not a reason to pick weaker models.
candidates.validation_test: Run the same injection suite across a current model family's small-to-large variants with task accuracy measured alongside, checking whether attack success still rises with capability.

reason: The paper measures prompt-injection success rates on 35 OpenAI example prompts with GPT-3, and reports which application-side settings reduce success. Two defensive configuration rules and one delimiter/sanitisation rule are actionable; other findings are descriptive.
